cover:
COVER · about 20s
• SAY: Good afternoon. I'm Hind, from Gold Coast Games, in Accra.
• ASK, then pause: Have you ever used a system that made perfect sense on paper, but was frustrating in real life?
• SAY: The process was there, the technology worked, but the human experience was missing. That is the human layer.
• NEXT: Let me introduce five people.
people:
FIVE PEOPLE · about 25s
• SAY: Ama's sign-off is trusted. Kofi wins the room. Yaw is who you trust with the long job. Efua is who you call when it has to move now. Selorm is who you send when nobody knows the way.
• CAREFUL: fictional working-style archetypes. Not personality tests, not a ranking, not labels that stick to a person.
• POINT OUT: the detailed numbers appear on their phones when they vote.
number:
GHANA 8% · about 30s
• SAY: In Ghana, by Gallup's measure, 8% of employees are engaged at work. Eight in a hundred.
• SAY: I don't think those 92 are lazy. I think we often give the right person the wrong job.
• CAREFUL: that is my interpretation. Gallup measures engagement, not the cause. Sub-Saharan Africa is 19%, global 20%. Data is 2025; Ghana's figure is a three-year rolling average.
• NEXT: So let's try something.
turnover:
EVERY EXIT RESTARTS A CLOCK · about 25s
• SAY: When someone leaves, or is let go, the business pays. Gallup puts replacement at half to twice annual salary, and a new hire can take about a year to reach peak performance.
• POINT OUT: this is the cost of a poor match between a person and the work.
• CAREFUL: US figures, and the slide says so. Say 'can', not 'always'. The 12 months is Gallup's own experience, an average, not a formal study. I have no Ghana number and will not invent one.
join:
JOIN · about 90s
• SAY: Scan once. It is the only code you need today. If you want to take part throughout the talk, keep that page open on your phone until the end. (Do not call it onboarding. Everything happens on that page, including the last step at the end.) The big screen shows totals, never names.
• POINT OUT (neighbours): if someone next to you is stuck, or not used to smartphones, they can answer on YOUR phone.
• WHY I BUILT IT THIS WAY: to show we can design for people who are not digital natives. In Africa that gap is huge, with a large pipeline of people without access or knowledge. We can design so they are not left out.
• STAT: at the 2021 census about 1 in 4 Ghanaians aged 15+ did not use the internet, and the share was higher for women (30%) than men (20%) (Ghana Statistical Service). That is who the neighbour feature is for.
• CAREFUL: half of you may see a countdown. Do not say which half. Fallback if wifi fails: show of hands. Close the join after about 90 seconds.
vote:
VOTE · about 90s with the reveal
• DO: say "You run technology at a bank." Tell it as a story, one panel at a time. Pause between panels. Ask for a show of hands: has something like this happened in your organisation?
• PANEL 1, 10:30pm: it is month-end. Your five-person team is each holding something critical: core banking, cards and ATMs, the mobile app, fraud monitoring, and regulatory reporting.
• PANEL 2, 11:10: partner companies send their payroll through your payments API. Their files are bouncing.
• PANEL 3, 11:25: the CFO calls. 40,000 salaries must be resubmitted before the morning cut-off. The vendor on call says the fault is in your setup, and only your team can change production.
• PANEL 4, 11:30: the incident manager can release one person. Everyone else stays on watch. Who do you pull? Thirty seconds.
• WHY ONE: the other systems need watching, only your own team can change production, and the cut-off is fixed. The job is hands-on and alone: find the fault in the gateway setup and fix it before the cut-off.
• AFTER THE REVEAL: expect Efua. Tonight is a sprint, hands-on, alone, against a hard deadline. Ask who picked differently: whoever they picked is defensible. Careful, steady people matter too, and that is the point.
• NO LABELS OR CLOCK ON THE SLIDE: the deadline, the time left and the one-person limit are all in the story. Let them work it out, do not add rules.
• CAREFUL: fictional bank, fictional people. Before the talk, have someone from a Ghanaian bank confirm the cut-off wording, the vendor's on-call access, and who decides who is released.
• NEXT: now change the job. A launch day for 300 agents, six people who have never met. Different job, different answer. Nobody is the best. The job decides.
shortlist:
THE RIGHT PEOPLE · about 25s · CONCEPT
• SAY: No one can hold the stats, skills and capacity of 100 people in their head. The system filters, so the people who fit are put forward, not overlooked.
• SAY: Leaders, admin or HR make the final decision, with room for human intuition. The system narrows. It does not decide.
• CAREFUL: say 'fewer overlooked', not 'none'. '100 people, 5 qualify' is an illustration with invented people. This part is a concept.
notjust:
THIS ISN'T JUST A CONCEPT · about 20s
• SAY: This is GCG Game Plan, the tool I use with my own team. I will not show you my people, so the names are blurred.
• POINT OUT: who said yes to which jobs; jobs nobody has picked yet; draft owners I review before anything is published.
• CAREFUL: launched recently, still rolling out. Say so. Replace the black box with your recording.
demo:
LIVE DEMO · about 70s
• DO: tap the gold button to open GCG Game Plan in a new tab. Ctrl+Tab, Cmd+Tab or Alt+Tab to come back. Use invented people only, never your real team.
• THE PROJECT TO PUT IN (one project, seven tasks): 1 Fix onboarding in five days (urgent, fast, one person alone). 2 Run the team offsite (a team, people, trust, a clear story). 3 Month-end report, never late (long, careful, consistent). 4 Find out why new customers go quiet (unclear brief). 5 Final quality sign-off (careful, detailed, alone). 6 Run the big screen and sound on the night (urgent, hands-on, a team). 7 Legal and compliance review (long, detailed, unclear rules, urgent).
• IF YOUR APP SHOWS A PATH: show a person seeing where they stand, what would close the gap (jobs to land, skills to learn) and who could help. That is step 5 on this slide. Say 'we aim to' for anything not built, including pairing someone with a helper.
• IF YOUR APP HAS TIERS AND LOAD: show tasks tagged easy, medium, hard or difficult, each person's baseline, and a maximum. Show a person who is at their maximum: to take a new job they swap one out or reassign it. Show an HR-agreed lower amount for the month, with the reason private. Remaining and overloaded work shows up for people to share. If this is not built yet, say 'we aim to'.
• IF BUILT, SHOW: someone at their maximum spotting a job they like, then swapping another out, or requesting more team members on a job.
• LEFTOVERS TO SHOW: the tasks nobody fits (up for grabs), and tasks someone has not finished. Show a person saying 'I am not finished' or asking for help, and adding a job within a job, if your app does that today. Then show the remaining list clearly, to share or to hire for. If a feature is not built yet, say 'we aim to'.
• WHAT IT SHOULD SHOW: for each task, the top person first, then the next, and the next, in order. If two people tie, both are highlighted. Tasks 1 to 5 each have a clear lead among your five people. Tasks 6 and 7 have no strong fit: they are UP FOR GRABS, to share or to hire for, so you can see what is left.
• SAY: it ranks, a person decides. You can pick someone lower. Promotions are decided by people, by published criteria, never by the system alone.
• FLEX: you took a while to pick for one task. The system filtered the whole project at once and showed the top five for each.
• CAREFUL: matching is rule-based today and the people are invented; AI is next. My guide is from the companion app's trait numbers, so your app's rankings may differ: run the project once and update slide 10 to match. Fallback: play the screen recording.
changed:
NOBODY GOT WORSE · about 40s
• SAY: I put one whole project into the system. It broke it into tasks and, for each task, ranked the people best first. I made the final call on each one.
• THE HUMAN LAYER, IN ONE BREATH (say it here, it is in the 10-minute run): the human layer to excellence takes human nature, error and life into account. That means building systems that allow for the natural states of being human: a pregnancy, grief, a celebration, a hard season, a mistake. People are not machines running at one speed. A system that cannot bend for life makes people hide it or leave. CAREFUL: say 'we aim to' for what is not built; the reason a person gives stays private; this is our view, not a research finding.
• ON THE SLIDE: three examples only. Efua leads the sprint, Kofi the offsite, Yaw the report that cannot be late, Ama signs off. The demo shows all five getting their jobs, so do not read out the rest. The job decides who leads and who covers.
• UNIVERSITY EXAMPLE (say after the up-for-grabs box): This is not only for companies. A group project has the same problem: who does what, who is stuck, what is left over. Here the students share with each other what they are good at and what they would like help with, so the team can split the work fairly and help each other. They choose what to share, and it is shared with their team, not published. A lecturer can see where a team needs support. Say 'we aim to' and 'could': this has not been used with students yet.
• UNIVERSITY CAREFUL: say 'what I'm strong at, what I'd like help with', not 'weaknesses'. Sharing is opt-in and team-only. Make clear it is not for grading. Student data is personal data (Act 843 and the university's own rules).
• BUSINESS MODEL (one sentence, only if asked or if it fits): we see individuals subscribing, with customised versions for companies and universities. No prices or dates unless decided.
• LEFT OVER: in a project we sometimes get lost. People take jobs, or we give people jobs, and some things cannot be done by anyone, or are not finished. They get left, and things turn chaotic. Here the system tracks what is not done yet or cannot be done. People can say 'I am not finished with this', ask for help or more people, or add a job within a job. We can see clearly what is still remaining, and share it between us.
• THE PATTERN: if a lot is left over, project after project, even after sharing, that points to a system problem, not a people problem. It may mean we need an extra person on the team for the work to function. That is how it shows us when to hire. CAREFUL: recurring leftovers are a signal, not proof; it could also be priorities or process. Say 'it can point to'. Say which of these features are built today and which are what we aim to build.
• TIERS, A BASELINE AND A MAXIMUM: tasks can have tiers: easy, medium, hard, difficult. Everyone takes a standard minimum at each tier, so the work is shared fairly. There is also a maximum. It is not a 'no'. A person says 'I am currently at my maximum', or 'I am overloaded right now', and the system shows their load. To take on a new job, they swap one out: reassign a job to someone who can take it, or take this one and hand another on. If someone has already spoken to HR and is going through a difficult time, they can set the amount of jobs they are taking this month, agreed with HR, and the reason stays private.
• EVEN AT MAXIMUM, PEOPLE CAN STILL MOVE: if someone sees a job they like, they can swap another job out. Or they can ask for more team members on a job: 'I need more people on this, can I request them?' They can also add a job within a job. The maximum is a flexible limit, not a wall.
• FAIRNESS CHECK: if people can swap into the jobs they like, the hard ones can get left behind. That is why the baseline minimum per tier and the leftover list matter, and a human approves swaps and requests. Say 'we aim to' for anything not built.
• WHAT IT TELLS US: if people keep hitting their maximum, or a lot is left over project after project, it points to a system problem, for example the team is too small and we may need to hire. It also helps us see who is genuinely compatible with the work, and reward them.
• DEVELOPMENT, NOT JUST DETECTION: the same data lets someone who is not up to par yet see where they are lacking, which they often cannot see for themselves. The system can show them: here is where you stand, here is what would close the gap, for example land this many jobs and learn this skill, and we can pair you with a person who can help. Then they can fit the job again. It helps with training people who are not there yet. Say it as a clear path and support, not as a warning.
• CAREFUL: 'at my maximum' is a signal to look at, never a verdict on the person. A person decides what a pattern means, after talking to the person. The reason stays private (a design commitment: your data is yours), and so does anything said to HR. Do not say 'we find the people who say no'. Avoid 'we might make you quit'; say 'here is the path and the help'. Have a Ghanaian lawyer check how this fits Act 843 and the Labour Act. Say which of this is built and which is 'we aim to'.
• FLEX: the first vote took the room a while to pick for one task. The system did the whole project at once. It surfaced the top five for every task, and I still chose.
• CAREFUL: these five people are invented; matching today is rule-based. This slide must match what you actually chose in the demo. If your demo gave different leads, change the names before you present.
three:
CUSTOMISE · OPTIMISE · GAMIFY · about 45s
• SAY: In this order. Customise first, and research comes first: we study the people, the culture and the place before we build.
• WHY CUSTOMISE: templates are built for the environment they came from, with fast internet and digitally fluent users, even digital nomads. Building in Ghana or Africa, we must remember that many people are not digitally inclined. A system that works somewhere else can leave our people out. So we customise to our real environment and our people.
• EXAMPLE, MOMO: in a very digitally inclined market you would not need so many mobile money vendors. Here, MoMo agents let people who cannot do it alone still use the system, and that is also how it grows. That is customising the environment through people. The question for us: what if we customise digitally too, as we can now?
• STAT, IF YOU WANT ONE (Ghana): at the 2021 census, about 1 in 4 people aged 15 and over, roughly 5 million (25.2%), did not use the internet. It was 30.3% of women against 19.8% of men, and above 50% in the Savannah, North East and Northern regions (Ghana Statistical Service, reported by Graphic Online, June 2023). A late-2025 estimate also puts about 1 in 4 Ghanaians offline (DataReportal, Digital 2026). Say 'roughly one in four', 'at the last census'.
• IF ASKED WHY: GSMA, as reported in September 2025: about 99% of Ghanaians are covered by a network, yet a 62% usage gap remains, and a smartphone costs about 27% of monthly GDP per capita, 76% for the poorest 40%. Check the GSMA report itself before quoting it.
• CAREFUL: offline is not the same as lacking digital skills. I found no Ghana digital-skills figure, so do not claim one.
• OPTIMISE: build on human nature. Right person, right job, right load.
• THE BIGGER AIM, SUSTAINABLE SYSTEMS: GCG exists to build systems that make sense. They are healthy and sustainable, they work, they are consistent, and they can scale. Say it as the test behind all three ideas, not as a fourth idea. CAREFUL: these are aims. The demo does not prove scaling, so say 'we aim to'.
• GAMIFY: clear progress and rewards, with healthy competition: against your own best and with one another, where everyone leads at something and nobody is ranked as a person.
• WHY MAKE IT FUN: You may be wondering how the platform works with gamification. Tonight was a small taste. Gamification is a process that helps: the aim is better systems, and rewarding people. Life does not have to be so boring, and neither do systems. Who told us they have to be? We spend most of our lives in them. Say a taste and a hint, not proof.
• HOW IT BECOMES A SYSTEM PEOPLE USE: This is a system we built through customisation. To make it one people actually use, take up and want to use, we build a reward system: we gamify it. People know there are pathways to promotion, and that being consistent on certain tasks, having good data, or being good at a certain task is recognised and rewarded.
• CAREFUL: say 'we aim to' for anything not built yet. Promotions are decided by people, by published criteria, never by the system alone.
• CAREFUL: say 'we aim to', not 'it improves'. 'Many people are not digitally inclined' and the MoMo point are my observations, not statistics. No numbers on MoMo agents unless you check them first.
glue:
GAME MECHANICS · about 25s
• SAY: Game mechanics turn passive users into active participants. They make boring or complicated systems more rewarding and easier to use.
• POINT OUT: three levels, customer-facing, employee-facing, business management. Filled chips are what you saw today. Outlined chips are also possible.
• CAREFUL: say 'can help', not 'will'. Rewards being earned and loyalty are what we aim for. Today's demo did not show them.
values:
WHAT WE VALUE · about 45s
• SAY: These are the values behind the culture we design for. Every one is a choice we build into the system.
• HUMAN EXCELLENCE (the backbone): the human layer to excellence takes human nature, error and life into account, so we build systems that allow for the natural states of humanity: pregnancy, grief, celebration and all the rest. the only way people can truly be excellent is if the system gives them a backbone for human error and hard seasons, so we work with the human, not against the human, and it is sustainable. Excellence is not squeezing more out of people; it is the conditions where their best can be repeated.
• EXAMPLE, SAY IT SLOWLY: in the app, a person can say they are going through a tough time, or a pregnancy. Because of their consistent work and the data already there, the system can give leeway: extra days off, or take things off their plate. We know this person is valuable and has worked hard, and right now they need support. Efua burns out on months of steady work; the system should notice and adjust.
• CAREFUL (privacy and law): the reason stays private. Health and pregnancy information is sensitive personal data, so have a Ghanaian lawyer check Act 843 and the Labour Act, including maternity protections, before you promise anything. Say 'we aim to'.
• CAREFUL (fairness): do not let care depend only on being a top performer. A sceptic may ask what about someone newer. Say support is for everyone, and a good track record is one way the system can offer more flexibility.
• HUMAN CONNECTION: people collaborate better, are understood and recognised, recognise each other, and become better team players. The system helps that happen; it does not force it.
• TEAMS FIRST: reward team effort, use all the team's capabilities wisely, build healthy team dynamics where people flourish. The best way to build something is together; each person does their own duties well, so they serve the system, the people and the team.
• HEALTHY COMPETITION (it is highlighted on purpose): we are a games company, so of course we love competition. We just design it to be healthy and fun. Competing with one another to do better is good, as long as it is not comparative. The winner is the winner for now; later someone else wins, and that is the point. Everyone leads at something, and the person who comes second often helps the winner. No names, no public ranking list. Ideas, not built: compete by skill and by period, let the lead change, recognise the people who helped.
• SUSTAINABLE SYSTEMS: the test behind all the others. Systems that make sense, stay healthy, work, stay consistent, have less friction, and can scale. These are aims; the demo does not prove scaling.
• IF ASKED ABOUT DATA (the commitments slide was cut, so say this in one breath): your data is yours, you can see it and edit it; scores are a signal for a person to review, never a verdict; rewards follow reviewed work, not activity; people decide, the system only filters. Say 'we aim to'. Have a Ghanaian lawyer check Act 843 before any legal claim.
• WORDING: say 'draw on people's strengths', not 'use people'.
choice:
WE HAVE A CHOICE · about 15s
• SAY: We have a choice. Left, we keep asking people to adapt to our systems. Right, we design systems intentionally to adapt to our people.
• DO: slow down. Do not answer it yet. Let the question sit.
whatchanged:
WHAT'S CHANGED · about 40s
• SLIDE IS DELIBERATELY SHORT: two sentences, no statistic. Say the rest.
• WHY NO STAT: the 15% to 56% figures measure how much faster people finish tasks with AI (customer support, a coding task). They do not measure the cost of customising a system, so they do not belong on this slide. 'AI makes customising more accessible' is my informed interpretation, not a published finding.
• IF ASKED FOR EVIDENCE: in studies, AI speeds up tasks by roughly 15% to 56% (see sources below). Say that is about task speed, not customisation specifically.
• ONE PERSON: 'within reach' means one person can now start. Say it aloud.
• SOURCES (not on the slide): Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, QJE 2025 (15%); Peng et al., 2023 (55.8%). Have these ready if asked.
• 1 BEFORE: it was more sustainable and convenient to use a set template. Customising was a lot of work. The payoff was real, but in practice only certain big organisations could afford it.
• 2 NOW: AI makes customising faster and more accessible. One person can start research a team once did. In studies, people finished tasks 15 to 56 percent faster.
• 3 WHY IT MATTERS HERE: templates are built for other environments. Here, many people are not digitally inclined. Think of MoMo agents: customising through people, because many cannot do it alone. Now we can customise digitally as well. Customising lets us design for them and for our real environment, and it is now within reach of small businesses too. We can use that to our advantage.
• CAREFUL: 15% is the published QJE paper (customer support issues per hour). 56% (55.8%) is one coding task in a lab. Different measures, so say 'in studies'. 'Only big organisations could afford it' is my reading, not a statistic.
• IF ASKED, COST: Stanford AI Index 2025, cost of running a GPT-3.5-level system fell over 280-fold (Nov 2022 to Oct 2024). That is running AI, not the cost of building a system.
• IF ASKED, SMALL BUSINESS: 58% of US small businesses used generative AI in 2025, up from 23% (US Chamber of Commerce). US data, measures use, not custom systems.
• IF ASKED, ACCURACY: AI speeds up desk research. It does not replace talking to people, and its output must be checked.
ask:
THE ASK · about 60s, then stay quiet while they tap
• SAY, slowly, then pause ten seconds: Which of your systems could benefit from game thinking? Think of one real system and one real team. Do not fill the silence.
• IF THEY LOOK BLANK: ask the warmer version aloud: where is your team quietly working around a system?
• SAY: Ten free consultations. Tap what you'd want us to look at: customer-facing, employee-facing, management systems. Pick as many as you like, then leave your email.
• CHOOSING THE TEN: not first come, first served. We choose the ten problems we are most interested in, where we can help build systems that work for people. Say only what you will do.
• NO PHONE OR QR? They can bring the problem to me after the talk, or write it down and email it. They are considered the same way.
• KEEP THE PAGE OPEN: do not call it onboarding. Say: if you want to take part throughout this talk, keep that page open on your phone until the end. Everything happens there.
• THEN: stop. Thirty seconds of silence while they tap.
• CAREFUL: say 'ten' only if you can honour ten. Decide beforehand what each one gets (for example a one-page game plan), by when, and on what grounds you choose, so the choice is fair and you can explain it.
final:
FINAL · stop talking
• THE IMAGE: all kinds of people playing, resting, racing, thinking, drumming at sunset. Do not explain it. If asked: that is who the systems are for.
• SAY the first line. Pause. Then the second: Let's lead the way in designing systems that work for our people.
• THEN: stop. Leave the slide up and take questions. Add nothing after 'our people'. The call is 'Let's'; the 10 free consultations on the slide before is how they act on it.
• CAREFUL: say 'for', not 'around'. 'Working around the system' is the negative idea from the ask slide.
